growth_story.headline: Japan's income per person has grown about 1.0 percent a year since 1990, slowly and with no lasting break, and reached a new high in 2025.
growth_story.arc: Japan's fastest growth came in the 1960s, when income per person grew by more than 10 percent in several years. Since 1990 the data show one long era with no lasting shift: growth averaged 1.0 percent a year over 1990–2025. The sources link the slow pace first to the bursting of the real estate and stock market bubble in the early 1990s and the bank troubles that followed, and later to a working-age population that has been shrinking since 1995. Sharp drops came with shocks: income per person fell 2.0 percent in 1998, 5.9 percent in 2009 when world demand collapsed, and 4.0 percent in 2020. The last two decades stayed close to the long average, at 0.7 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 0.8 percent over 2016–2025. Income per person reached its highest level so far in 2025, at 38,619 in constant dollars, after growth of 1.7 percent that year.

threads.title: Burst bubble, wary banks
threads.text: The sources date Japan's long slowdown to the bursting of its real estate and stock market bubble in the early 1990s. One study ties the slow years that followed partly to banks that grew wary of lending to small and new firms. Income per person shrank in 1993 and again in 1998 and 1999.

threads.title: A shrinking, aging workforce
threads.text: Japan's working-age population peaked in 1995 and has been shrinking since, which the IMF says has long kept growth subdued. Automation has helped hold up output per worker, and the IMF links the push for higher productivity to the aging population.

citations.quote: A shrinking and aging workforce has led to subdued GDP growth over the past two decades, but automation has supported labor productivity.

citations.title: Japan: 2026 Article IV Consultation-Press Release; Staff Report; and Statement by the Executive Director for Japan
citations.quote: Japan’s working age population (aged 15-64) peaked in 1995 and has been shrinking by approximately 0.6 percent per year since.

citations.quote: structural policies to improve efficiency and productivity in the context of an aging population

threads.title: Hit by world demand
threads.text: When world demand collapsed in 2008–09, Japan fell into what the IMF called its most severe recession in decades. Income per person fell 5.9 percent in 2009, the deepest drop in data that start in 1960, then grew 4.1 percent in 2010.

citations.title: 2009 Article IV Consultation with Japan: Concluding Statement of the IMF Mission
citations.quote: The collapse in external demand and financial spillovers have plunged the economy into the most severe recession in decades.

threads.title: Deflation ends, real wages fall
threads.text: After decades of prices that barely rose, inflation has run above the central bank's target for several years. Nominal wages are growing at their fastest in decades, but prices have risen faster, so real wages have fallen since 2022.

threads.text: The IMF expects spending on interest and on health and care for an older population to keep rising. It projects that this will push the public debt ratio up again from 2035.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 1.7 percent in 2025, after 0.2 percent in 2024, and reached a new high. A trade deal with the United States in July 2025 helped avert a bigger rise in US tariffs, and the harm from higher tariffs fell mostly on carmakers. Inflation eased in early 2026, and the IMF expects growth to slow in 2026 as world demand weakens and the conflict in the Middle East weighs on the outlook.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes total output, which it says shrank in 2024 because of temporary supply disruptions. Yet income per person rose 0.2 percent that year, because there were fewer people to share it. The same gap runs through the whole period: a shrinking workforce holds down total output, as the sources stress, while a shrinking population props up income per person, which has averaged 1.0 percent a year since 1990.
